task_statement:
Research question (as posed on 2026-10-06, in the area of defensive suppression and counter strategy (best/avoid)):
A defense's effect on opponents' H2-H1 change is a reliable team trait.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.
- Units available to a study of this question (as recorded): 120 team-seasons

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

research_concepts: second-half minus first-half change in opponent scoring (H2-H1)
methodological_questions: Is a team's defensive effect on opponents' H2-H1 change stable across split halves or seasons?
What number of team-seasons and games is needed to estimate that effect with useful reliability?
How much of the observed H2-H1 variation is regression to the mean or half-to-half noise?
Do foul trouble, free-throw mix, leakage, and pace confound H2-H1 comparisons?

historical_evidence.finding: Connector teammate-path quality Q_p split-half reliability (n=102 connectors): Pearson r=+0.215 (p=0.0297), Spearman rho=+0.242, Spearman-Brown about 0.355, sign agreement 65.7%, ICC(player-season)=0.216 with 78.4% of variance within player. Recorded failure evidence: split-half r=0.215 is too low to treat the measure as a stable scoutable trait. Mechanism recorded as A_unanswerable; limited by low measurement reliability.

Ranked playsheet validation over 10 series: Spearman rho=-0.0639 (p=0.0997, n=665), no clear full-rank signal. Kruskal-Wallis H=32.97 (p=2.7e-05). BEST mean 1.257 (n=56) vs AVOID 1.092 (n=160), U=5546, p=0.004. Trigger accuracy rho=0.4525 (n=121). Limited by leakage, low measurement reliability, and small sample; risks recorded as drift/nonstationarity, leakage, measurement reliability, and sample size.

Foul-trouble sequencing after a star's second Q1/Q2 foul: raw lag-1 effect +0.204 (CI +0.163 to +0.245) was produced by free-throw share (41.8% treated vs 9.9% control). Excluding free throws, lag-1 was +0.0486 (CI -0.006 to +0.099, perm p=0.0655), and no lag cleared CI, permutation, and placebo checks. Recorded mechanism: C_artifact; confounding.

Possession Control Index incremental R2 over ORtg: headline dR2=+0.139 was driven by leakage correlated with DRtg (corr=+0.894). Offensive-control components added only +0.005 R2 beyond ORtg. Baseline omitted defense by construction. n=120 team-seasons, out-of-sample 2025-26 with 30 teams.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Split-half reliability of a derived per-player on-off style measure used as a stable trait
failed_approaches.why: Low reliability (r=0.215, Spearman-Brown 0.355); most variance was within-player half-to-half, so the measure could not be treated as a stable trait.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Lagged opponent PPP after a star's second foul, using all possessions including free throws
failed_approaches.why: Apparent effect was a construction artifact from the free-throw mix; after removing free throws no lag passed the CI, permutation, and placebo tests.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Incremental-R2 claim for a control index over a Net-Rating baseline that omitted defense
failed_approaches.why: Gain came from leakage that tracked the defensive outcome (corr +0.89), so the baseline was mechanically incomplete rather than the index adding information.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Ranked playsheet counter prediction from H1-to-H2 play-type drops
failed_approaches.why: Full-rank Spearman was null (rho=-0.064, p=0.10); only a pairwise BEST vs AVOID difference emerged, with leakage, low reliability, and small samples recorded as limits.

evidence_establishes: Within this project's earlier work, split-half reliability of a derived per-entity measure in the NBA data was low (r about 0.2 with n=102), and it was judged insufficient for a stable trait claim ([prior work][prior work]).

Half-to-half and game-level noise in derived NBA halves/splits has produced artifacts and null results when the measure was built from play-by-play without strict controls (FAM:[prior work], [prior work][prior work], [prior work][prior work]).
Free-throw mix and leakage are documented confounders in this project's possession-level analyses (FAM:[prior work], [prior work][prior work]).
evidence_does_not_establish: No retrieved record tests whether a team's defensive effect on opponents' H2-H1 change is reliable. [prior work][prior work] concerns connector players, not team defense or H2-H1 change.
No retrieved record reports a team-level split-half or cross-season reliability for any defensive measure.
No retrieved record gives the sample size needed for a team-level H2-H1 reliability estimate with 120 team-seasons.
[prior work] do not show whether the 2022-23 to 2025-26 seasons have stable rules or coaching patterns that would make cross-season comparison valid.
own_inferences: H2-H1 is a difference of two noisy half-game measures. Its reliability will be lower than either half's reliability, so a team trait claim is harder to support than for the halves alone.
120 team-seasons means about 30 teams over 4 seasons, with repeated teams, so teams are not independent units and cross-season effective sample size is smaller than 120.
Team-level H2-H1 effects are likely dominated by game-level and situational noise (foul trouble, free-throw share, garbage time, pace, opponent quality) unless these are explicitly controlled.
The question as posed asks for reliability, but the naive test (correlate team H2-H1 effects across seasons) would also pick up stable team quality and style, not only the defensive-trait claim.
uncertainties: The full text of the retrieved records was not read (read_family not called), so exact n, controls, and thresholds beyond the summaries are unknown.
[prior work][prior work] was referenced as related by [prior work][prior work] but was not returned by retrieval and is not cited.
Data-level details such as how H1/H2 are defined in overtime and how partial possessions enter the team-level effect are not in the task statement.
Whether 2025-26 playoff data (complete as of 2026-06-21) is comparable to regular-season data is unknown.

historical_effect.explanation: Without the retrieved records the question could have been pre-registered as a plain cross-season correlation test. The prior low-reliability result ([prior work][prior work]) and the foul and leakage artifacts (FAM:[prior work], [prior work][prior work]) show that a derived split-based measure from this data is likely to be noisy and artifact-prone. That supports a reliability-first gate before any claim that the trait is real, rather than proceeding directly to the effect test.

blocking_constraints.text: The H2-H1 effect is a difference of two noisy halves; reliability of the team-level estimate is not shown to be adequate, and [prior work][prior work] found low reliability for a similar derived measure.
120 team-seasons (about 30 teams x 4 seasons) is a small, non-independent sample for detecting a stable team trait in a noisy difference score.
Foul trouble, free-throw share, pace, opponent strength, and garbage time can drive H2-H1 differences (FAM:[prior work]).

prior_work.summary: No retrieved record answers whether team defensive effects on opponents' H2-H1 change are reliable. The closest record ([prior work][prior work]) shows low split-half reliability for a different per-player measure with n=102. Other records show artifacts and nulls from related play-by-play constructions, supporting caution about confounding and leakage.

risks.text: Difference-score reliability of H2-H1 is likely low; [prior work][prior work] found low reliability for a comparable derived measure.
120 team-seasons with repeated teams gives limited effective sample size for a trait claim.
Free-throw mix, foul trouble, pace, opponent quality, and garbage time can produce H2-H1 differences unrelated to defense (FAM:[prior work]).
Any defensive measure built from the same game's second half can leak outcome information into the H2-H1 estimate ([prior work][prior work], [prior work][prior work]).
Team defense and opponent scoring are mechanically linked to net rating, so a defensive H2-H1 effect can partly reflect shared scoring structure ([prior work][prior work]).
Selecting teams with extreme H2-H1 defensive effects in one season and testing them in another will overstate persistence.
Rule, pace, and coaching changes across 2022-23 to 2025-26 can shift H2-H1 patterns, weakening cross-season reliability ([prior work][prior work]).
Multiple split definitions, play types, and H2-H1 variants increase the chance of a spurious reliable-trait result.
Low base rates of true team-level H2-H1 differences would make a positive reliability claim hard to support at this sample size.

design.estimand: Minimum viable test: reliability of team-level defensive effect on opponents' H2-H1 PPP change, estimated as split-half (odd/even games within season) and cross-season intraclass correlation, with a Spearman-Brown correction. Only if reliability is adequate should a trait claim follow.
design.unit: Team-season (30 teams x 4 seasons, about 120 units), with games nested within team-season; also game-level for split-half estimates.
design.sample: NBA 2022-23 to 2024-25 regular seasons (complete) plus 2025-26 regular season only from 2026-04-13 onward; playoffs excluded from the reliability test or analysed separately. Freeze the data version before analysis; 2025-26 playoffs are complete as of 2026-06-21 but should not be pooled without a comparability check.
design.power: Before analysis, simulate the sampling distribution of split-half and cross-season ICC at 120 team-seasons. Proceed to a trait claim only if the lower 95% bound of reliability exceeds a pre-set threshold (for example 0.5); otherwise report as untestable at this sample size.
design.controls: Adjust H2-H1 for free-throw share, foul counts, pace, opponent strength, and garbage-time filtering (margin threshold). Exclude possessions after the first 'garbage' margin. Use defensive matchup minutes for opponent-adjusted estimates. Avoid any leakage: define the defensive measure from data available before the H2 window it is compared against.
design.falsification: Pre-register that a reliability ICC below threshold, or a null correlation between split-half estimates, falsifies the trait claim. Include a placebo H1-H1 split (first half versus an earlier split) to check whether the reliability is specific to H2-H1 or reflects generic team quality.
design.multiplicity: Pre-register one primary reliability estimate (odd/even games within season, cross-season ICC). Treat other play types and H2-H1 variants as exploratory with Holm correction.
design.decision_rule: Support a trait claim only if the primary split-half and cross-season reliabilities both exceed the pre-set threshold, the H1-H1 placebo does not show the same reliability, and the effect survives the free-throw, foul, pace, and garbage-time adjustments. Otherwise report as uncertain or untestable.
design.data_version: Frozen NBA stats API play-by-play, substitution, starters, and matchup-minute files as of 2026-10-06; 2025-26 regular season used only after 2026-04-13 completion; 2025-26 playoffs excluded from the primary analysis, with the versioned extract recorded.
